explanation.keyIdea: A dynamic arc is shaped by more than loudness. A fingerstyle arrangement can grow through a fuller arpeggio, a higher melody register, longer sustain or a denser bass pattern, then become sparse again. The pulse and harmony can stay stable while texture and touch guide the listener through the piece.
explanation.plainLanguage: Start with a quiet, simple version of the idea. Add more notes or a higher melody in the middle, then return to the opening texture. Keep the tempo steady; make the music grow through touch and arrangement rather than speeding up.
explanation.workedExample: Use G–Cadd9–Em7–Dsus4/D. Bars 1–2: soft bass plus one treble note per bar. Bars 3–4: even p–i–m–a arpeggios. Bars 5–6: add a clearer upper melody and fuller treble response. Bars 7–8: return to the sparse opening texture and finish on G.

demonstrationOrReference.referenceSuggestion: Use original GuitarLab demonstrations or teacher-created examples. Demonstrate relaxed free-stroke finger motion and, where appropriate, a light rest-stroke melody touch without requiring nails, a fixed wrist angle or one universal hand shape. steps: Choose the progression G (320003), Cadd9 (x30010), Em7 (022033), Dsus4 (xx0233) resolving to D (xx0232).
Play the progression softly with only the bass note and one upper melody note; this is the opening texture.
Repeat with a full p–i–m–a arpeggio at a moderate dynamic while keeping the same tempo.
In bars 5–6, add a higher melody note or fuller treble response and slightly stronger attack; do not force the volume or increase the tempo.
In bars 7–8, reduce the texture back to bass plus one upper note and resolve to G with a controlled note length.
Record the eight bars and listen for a clear dynamic arc, balanced bass and melody, and an intentional final decay.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: The music gets louder only because the player attacks harder and loses tone control.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: The ending stops abruptly rather than returning to the opening idea.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Reintroduce the sparse texture and plan the final G note's length and decay.

learningObjectives: Plan an original eight- to sixteen-bar acoustic piece with a clear section order, chord progression, recurring melody and intentional ending.

explanation.keyIdea: The capstone combines the route's parts into one musical arrangement. The thumb supports the harmony, upper fingers shape an arpeggio or melody, bass movement connects chords, and chord colour or open-string resonance adds character. A coherent arrangement is more important than demonstrating every technique in every bar; choose features that support the melody and keep the form clear.
explanation.plainLanguage: Make a short original acoustic piece. Let the bass and fingers work together, give the listener a melody or recurring idea, use one colour change, shape the music from simple to fuller and back, and finish deliberately. Record it and choose one thing to improve rather than chasing speed.
explanation.workedExample: One possible eight-bar framework: C | G/B | Am | G | Cadd9 | G/B | Am | G. Use a p–i–m–a arpeggio as the base texture; keep the descending C–B–A–G bass line clear; sing and add a short upper melody; use Cadd9 for a colour change; add one soft muted brush only if it supports the groove; return to the opening texture and resolve to G.

steps: Choose an original eight- to sixteen-bar form. One option is C–G/B–Am–G repeated twice, with a melody or riff that returns in the second half.

explanation.keyIdea: Guitar TAB maps strings and fret numbers. The top line is the thinnest string (high E), the bottom line is the thickest string (low E), and a number tells you the fret to play; 0 means an open string. Staff notation is a parallel, optional way to represent pitch and rhythm.

exercises.title: Listen, name and prepare
instructions: Say what you are trying to make sound or demonstrate.
Listen to a reference or hum the target before playing.
Choose a comfortable starting tempo and one observable quality target.
exercises.successCriterion: You can state the target and identify what a successful attempt should sound or feel like.

exercises.title: Focused skill drill
instructions: Perform the selected excerpt from count-in to ending without stopping. If a mistake occurs, keep the pulse and rejoin at the next safe point.
Work in short sets; pause to identify and correct one specific issue before repeating.
Only increase tempo after clean, relaxed repetitions; reduce it if accuracy or comfort declines.
exercises.successCriterion: The learner completes the form, maintains the pulse or recovers musically, and identifies one specific strength and one next target.

exercises.title: Musical application
instructions: Apply the week's exercise: Create or perform an original 4- to 8-bar example demonstrating path capstone..
Play a short phrase, loop or section with a count-in and intentional ending.
Where possible, combine the new skill with one familiar skill while preserving the pulse.
exercises.successCriterion: Demonstrate this week's checkpoint: Demonstrate path capstone in a short musical example, explain the key choice and identify one next improvement.

exercises.title: Recall and reflect
instructions: Put the diagram or notes away and answer the retrieval prompts.
Record one thing that improved and one issue that still needs attention.
Choose whether the next session should repeat, simplify, mix or extend the task.
exercises.successCriterion: A clear next target is recorded and the concept can be recalled without immediately viewing the explanation.

musicalApplication.prompt: Create or perform an original 4- to 8-bar example demonstrating path capstone.
instructions: Count in before beginning.
Play the entire short phrase or loop without stopping for a small error.
Repeat once with attention to the weakest quality, not simply at a higher speed.
musicalApplication.sourcePolicy: Use original GuitarLab examples, learner-created material or properly licensed/public-domain repertoire; link to commercial song tabs rather than copying them.

successCriteria.criterion: The learner reproduces the contour and rhythm, locates the intended notes with a deliberate checking process, and can explain what was uncertain.
The notes or chords are clear enough for the task and the pulse remains understandable.
Movement remains relaxed; stop and reset if pain, numbness or tingling occurs.
The learner can explain the key idea and apply it in the week's musical example.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Stopping every time a note is missed.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Practise re-entry points and keep counting through small errors.

commonMistakesAndCorrections.mistake: Changing many things at once after listening to a recording.
commonMistakesAndCorrections.correction: Choose one observable target per review take, such as timing, transition or dynamics.

lessons.accessibleAlternative: Record a shorter section or audio-only take; use a click count-in and mark the form on paper.

nextReviewSuggestion.approach: Adaptive retrieval; suggested intervals are configurable product heuristics, not scientifically optimal fixed intervals.
suggestedChecks: Next practice session: recall the concept before viewing this lesson.
About one week later: repeat the task without the original step-by-step prompt.
About one month later: apply the skill in a different progression, rhythm or musical context.
nextReviewSuggestion.adaptation: Review sooner after errors, hesitation, low confidence or loss of control; extend the interval after confident retrieval on separate occasions.

fortyMinutes: 5 min: prepare and review a related skill
15 min: focused drill in short sets
10 min: new learning or extension
7 min: musical application
3 min: reflect
practiceOptions.rule: Select the highest-value tasks for the time available; do not rush every activity into a short session.

instructorNotes.pacing: Repeat or split the lesson across sessions until the learner can demonstrate the target reliably. Week numbers are an ordering aid, not a calendar deadline.
instructorNotes.tempoGuidance: The outline tempo of 60 BPM is a reference only. Begin slower if needed; increase only after accuracy and comfort remain steady.
instructorNotes.masteryBoundary: Lesson completion, time spent and video viewing do not equal mastery. Record evidence separately and require more than one successful demonstration over time for a stable skill.

lessons.checkpoint: Demonstrate path capstone in a short musical example, explain the key choice and identify one next improvement.
